title: Gagasan Nadi Cergas builds on affordable housing niche to drive earnings growth
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on February 2, 2026 - February 8, 2026
CONSTRUCTION player and property developer Gagasan Nadi Cergas Bhd (KL: NADIBHD ) has carved a niche for itself in the affordable housing segment, positioning the company for strong earnings growth on the back of a solid project pipeline.
It is committed to delivering more than 15,000 affordable homes over the next eight years, with an estimated gross development value (GDV) of RM4.1 billion.
Its affordable housing projects are located in four key townships across Selangor — Kwasa Damansara, City of Elmina, Bandar Rimbayu and Bukit Jelutong — under the state government’s Rumah Idaman initiative. The size of the homes ranges from 1,000 to 1,120 sq ft while the selling prices are between RM250,000 and RM290,000.
To date, the 1,260-unit Idaman Bukit Jelutong project, with an estimated GDV of RM304 million, has been completed and had achieved a take-up rate of 98% as at end-September 2025.
In an interview with The Edge, Gagasan Nadi Cergas founder and managing director Datuk Wan Azman Wan Kamal says the government policy on affordable housing, including the requirement for developers to allocate 20% of their projects to affordable homes, has significantly expanded the group’s portfolio.
“We are working closely with the Selangor government on the Rumah Idaman initiative, delivering partially furnished three or four-bedroom homes,” explains Wan Azman, who owns a 64.69% stake in the company and has nearly 40 years of experience in the property development and construction industry.
Wan Azman, who had founded the company in 1999, says it has increasingly partnered developers to fulfil its affordable housing obligations, creating a win-win situation.
“Many developers who own land earmarked for affordable housing approach us to help them deliver on their commitments to the state government,” he adds.
While Gagasan Nadi Cergas is currently focused on the Selangor affordable housing market, Wan Azman says it is open to exploring opportunities in other states such as Penang and Johor. However, he rules out the possibility of undertaking landed affordable housing due to compressed margins.
“It is not economical for us to do landed affordable housing. High-rise projects allow us to achieve a density of 120 units per acre,” he says.
The company also has several projects in Kuala Lumpur and Ulu Yam, Selangor, with a combined estimated GDV of more than RM700 million that are scheduled to be launched later.
As at end-September 2025, the group’s property development division had recorded unbilled sales of RM203 million, which are expected to be recognised as revenue over the next three years.
Addressing concerns about the property glut, Wan Azman maintains that this is not an issue for the company because of its focus on prime locations.
“Overhang does happen, but not in the areas that we develop. For example, our Kwasa Damansara projects are within walking distance of MRT stations,” he explains.
Unlike its peers, Gagasan Nadi Cergas follows an asset-light model in which it partners landowners in property projects instead of acquiring land outright. The company owns 128.4 acres and an additional 172.6 acres with development rights.
Listed on Bursa Malaysia’s ACE Market, Gagasan Nadi Cergas is targeting a transfer to the Main Market this year.
“With higher earnings, we are aiming to apply for a listing transfer upon completing our audit,” Wan Azman says.
From its listing price of 30 sen apiece, the stock was up 36.7% last Thursday. It ended trading at 41 sen, giving the company a market capitalisation of RM308.73 million.
Gagasan Nadi Cergas is trading at a price-earnings ratio of 16.2 times, substantially higher than that of its peers, such as LBS Bina Group Bhd (KL: LBS ) (6.5 times), WCT Holdings Bhd (KL: WCT ) (9.4 times) and Paramount Corp Bhd (KL: PARAMON ) (5.6 times), according to AskEdge data.
For the first nine months ended Sept 30, 2025 (9MFY2025), Gagasan Nadi Cergas’ net profit tripled to RM19.14 million from RM5.82 million a year ago, driven by higher recognition of property development projects and improved cost efficiency in construction operations. Property development accounted for about 70% of profit before tax during the period.
In FY2024, net earnings more than doubled to RM5.87 million from RM2.43 million a year ago.
Moving forward, the group’s profitability will be supported by an external construction order book of RM221 million as well as internally generated construction works from its own property development activities.
As a Grade G7 contractor, Gagasan Nadi Cergas is eligible to bid for projects of unlimited value, including bumiputera-allocated projects. Its current tender book exceeds RM1 billion.
“Usually, the chances of getting design-and-build projects are higher than conventional tenders because only a select few contractors are invited to submit bids due to the high requirements.
“For example, for our PFI (private finance initiative) projects, we need to have a paid-up capital of RM20 million to RM30 million, with financing capped at 80% while the balance 20% is funded through equity. We are currently handling a few PFI projects, to be specific, student accommodation as well as government projects like hospitals and police stations,” Wan Azman says.
Among its completed projects in recent years are Masjid Al-Sultan Abdullah in Kuala Lumpur and the Serdang Hospital Cardiology Centre in Selangor.
The group remains unfazed by rising raw material prices, citing flexibility in pricing adjustments. The prices of some housing units have been revised upwards to RM290,000 from RM250,000.
“Building material prices are forecast to increase 2% to 3% this year because of higher transport costs and other factors. The state government has been very understanding, allowing us to increase our prices for slightly larger units as they recognise the need for developers to remain viable under the affordable housing programme,” Wan Azman says.
To strengthen its concession and facility management segment, Wan Azman says the group is looking for more merger and acquisition (M&A) opportunities following its recent acquisition of student hostel concessionaire Konsortium PAE Sepakat Sdn Bhd for RM127.3 million.
This acquisition grants the group a 10-year facility management concession for student hostels across seven polytechnic campuses in the country, serving 10,000 students.
In addition, the group holds two ongoing 20-year concessions to maintain the student hostels of International Islamic University Malaysia in Kuantan and Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka until 2034 and 2037 respectively. These concessions are expected to generate more than RM500 million in receivables over the remaining concession period. This is on top of a RM174 million order book to be recognised as revenue when services are delivered on a monthly basis, says Wan Azman.
“There is a very high degree of certainty in the concession segment as we receive fixed income from the government every month. Whether or not there are students staying in the hostels, it still pays us the same amount,” he adds.
Meanwhile, the group’s utilities segment operates 30-year concessions until 2051 to 2052 to distribute electricity and supply chilled water to the Datum Jelatek Mall in Kuala Lumpur.
In view of its strong earnings outlook, the group plans to “reactivate” its dividend payout in 4QFY2025 with a targeted dividend policy of up to 30%, following its last dividend payment in FY2020.
As at end-September 2025, Gagasan Nadi Cergas was in a net cash position of RM20.64 million given cash and bank balances of RM148.96 million against RM128.32 million in borrowings.

title: Impala Platinum expects half-year profit to surge by 400% on metals rally
body:
(Feb 3): Impala Platinum Holdings Ltd said its second-half profit likely jumped by about 400% from a year earlier because of the rally in metals.
A “significant appreciation” in the average price received for the firm’s products is behind the better performance, the Johannesburg-listed miner of platinum group metals said on Tuesday in a trading statement. Earnings are expected to be between 9.1 billion rand (RM2.22 billion) and 9.45 billion rand.
Implats, as the company is known, and its South African peers will soon announce results for last year. Platinum almost doubled in the six months through December, while palladium rose about 66%. Both metals continued to climb in 2026 until paring most of this year’s gains last week in a broader slump for precious metals.
Valterra Platinum Ltd — which until recently was a subsidiary of Anglo American plc — said in January it expects the firm’s profit last year increased by as much as 125% to 15.9 billion rand.
The biggest source of demand for platinum and palladium — the two main PGMs — is in devices that lower harmful emissions from gasoline and diesel vehicles. Producers are focused on finding alternative sources of demand to offset the growing market share of electric vehicles, which do not use the metals.
South Africa is by far the world’s largest supplier of platinum.

title: KIP REIT doubles down on neighbourhood malls, eyeing RM2 bil AUM
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on February 2, 2026 - February 8, 2026
KIP Real Estate Investment Trust (KL: KIPREIT ) has been on the lookout for more community-centric retail properties to boost its assets under management (AUM) to RM2 billion by 2027. The REIT’s manager says its pipeline of prospective properties remains “healthy” despite asset prices inching higher.
“We are aggressively reviewing the potential of the proposed properties. We remain laser-focused on acquiring assets in the retail space, where our resources lie,” KIP REIT Management Sdn Bhd CEO Valerie Ong Pui Shan tells The Edge.
“From a strategic perspective, we are attracted to regions with growth potential, especially those with a strong residential catchment, including new suburban areas, which we are very keen to explore.”
New acquisitions need to deliver targeted yields of between 6.5% and 7%, according to Ong. Apart from location and catchment strength, other key considerations include income stability, tenant resilience, yield accretion, funding structure and impact on gearing levels.
“We are optimistic about reaching the RM2 billion AUM milestone within the targeted time frame,” she says, noting that the group could potentially exceed its target, subject to market conditions.
KIP REIT’s AUM currently stands at RM1.7 billion. Its portfolio comprises 12 retail malls and six industrial properties across Perak, Selangor, Pahang, Negeri Sembilan, Melaka, Johor and Sarawak.
The REIT has headroom of RM200 million for acquisitions without diluting shareholder value, based on its internal gearing cap of 45% and gearing ratio of about 39% as at end-December last year.
“The regulatory threshold is 50%, but we don’t want to exceed 45% to ensure that there is some financial flexibility for us. Funding will be a mix of bank borrowings and equity,” says Ong.
“Any acquisition will be assessed strictly on a yield-accretive and earnings-enhancement basis. It must translate into tangible value creation. We will not pursue transactions that compromise our balance sheet strength or unitholder returns.”
Once its RM2 billion AUM target is achieved, the REIT manager will focus on asset optimisation, says Ong. “With scale secured, the focus will shift from buying assets to optimising them, and allowing the assets to deliver their full upside. This will position us well to compound returns and create long-term value for our unitholders.”
KIP REIT’s financial performance has been robust. In the first half of its financial year 2026 (1HFY2026) ended Dec 31, 2025, its net property income (NPI) surged 50.5% year on year to RM62.13 million from RM41.29 million, driven by higher contribution from the DPulze Shopping Centre in Cyberjaya and KIPMall Desa Coalfields in Sungai Buloh, Selangor. Revenue increased 48.6% to RM84.24 million from RM56.71 million.
Analysts say the results were in line with market expectations. CIMB Securities expects the REIT’s earnings to improve quarter on quarter in 3QFY2026 on higher footfall resulting from the Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (Sara) cash aid, the reopening of KIPMall Tampoi in Johor following asset enhancement works and the festive season.
Meanwhile, TA Securities expects the reduction in the sales and service tax (SST) on rents, from 8% to 6%, to be broadly positive for KIP REIT. Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) with annual sales not exceeding RM1.5 million are exempted from service tax on rental services. SMEs account for about 31% of the REIT’s tenant base.
As at end-December 2025, KIP REIT had RM662.2 million in borrowings and RM55.94 million in cash and cash equivalents. It raised just over RM130 million by placing out 160 million units in August and October last year, with proceeds bolstering its deal headroom and supporting its acquisitions of KIPMall Desa Coalfields and KIP Kuantan that were completed in August and September last year respectively.
KIP REIT’s distribution per unit was 3.5 sen for 1HFY2026, higher than the 3.18 sen in 1HFY2025. It made a distribution per unit of 6.8 sen in FY2025, which translates into a distribution yield of more than 7%. Note that REITs are required to distribute at least 90% of their income to be tax-exempt.
KIP REIT’s unit price had risen 13.7% over the past year to close at 93.5 sen last Tuesday, giving the REIT a market value of RM896.3 million.
Its retail segment contributed 94% to its revenue in 1HFY2026. Ong says the REIT’s community-centric neighbourhood malls, which cater to the mass market, are expected to continue delivering resilient growth.
“Our 12 shopping malls are very similar in nature in terms of geography and demographics. That’s why they are able to be sustainable in our space,” she adds.
Ong says the retail operations — such as supermarkets, pharmacies, and food and beverage outlets — that cater to people’s daily needs remain structurally defensive, supported by stable population growth and recurring consumption of essential categories. “As consumer behaviour evolves, the role of neighbourhood malls as convenient and accessible community hubs has become increasingly important.”
On future acquisitions, Ong hopes to replicate its success story at DPulze Shopping Centre in Cyberjaya, which achieved a yield of 10% in just nine months post-acquisition, up from 7.1% when the deal was announced in May 2024.
Notably, DPulze, which has full occupancy, contributed more than 24% to KIP REIT’s revenue in 1HFY2026. The occupancy rate across its entire portfolio stood at 98.2% at end-December 2025.
Ong stresses the importance of asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) in keeping its retail assets relevant. KIP Mall Tampoi in Johor is scheduled for reopening on Feb 8 after undertaking a transformation exercise, while KIP Mall Masai has been identified as the next AEI candidate. Meanwhile, the REIT is expanding its footprint with AEON Kinta City in Ipoh, Perak, through the construction of a new annex building.
On its assets in the industrial segment, Ong acknowledges that the growing supply in recent years warrants caution, particularly in certain locations and subsegments. Nevertheless, she notes that long-term demand continues to be supported by structural trends such as e-commerce growth, supply chain diversification and manufacturing relocation.
Having said that, she notes that rising land prices have made it increasingly challenging to secure high-yielding industrial properties.
“Moving forward, I think it will not be as easy [to acquire industrial properties], because land prices have gone up significantly. It’s difficult to find assets with yields of 6.5% to 7%,” says Ong, adding that preferred industrial assets are those located in industrial parks and close to ports.
KIP REIT has adopted a “2+2” rental model to balance income visibility and flexibility in a volatile environment, allowing for more frequent rental repricing while maintaining continuity through renewal options.
Across its portfolio, recent rental reversions have been encouraging, at 5% to 10% for retail assets. Rental reversions can reach 15% to 20%, with gross turnover (GTO) increasingly embedded into renewal of leases to better align with the upside of tenant performance and capture an additional lift in earnings. On the other hand, rental reversions for industrial assets average about 10% to 12% per term, typically 12 to 15 years.
“I have instructed the team to incorporate GTO into all renewal cases, so there will be more upside for the REIT,” says Ong.
As at end-December 2025, KIP REIT was managing about 3.2 million sq ft of net lettable area, with a diversified tenant base of 1,300, including nine supermarket operators. “All the tenants have been asking for additional space and more locations,” she says.
KIP REIT was among the big winners at The Edge Malaysia Centurion Club Corporate Awards 2025, clinching a hat-trick in the REIT category for Highest Growth In Profit After Tax Over Three Years, Highest Returns To Shareholders Over Three Years and Highest Return On Equity Over Three Years.
Hextar Group CEO Datuk Eddie Ong Choo Meng is the largest holder of KIP REIT units at 8.76%. KIP REIT co-founder and managing director Datuk Ong Kook Liong — Valerie’s father — has the second-largest holding at 7.47%.
Eddie’s sister, Michelle Ong Tzu Chuen, sits on the board as an executive director. Other major holders of KIP REIT units include AIA Bhd (4.38%) and the Employees Provident Fund (4.02%).

title: Alpha IVF says worst of start-up pains is over, still eyes regional expansion
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on February 2, 2026 - February 8, 2026
FERTILITY care specialist Alpha IVF Group Bhd (KL: ALPHA ) is doubling down on regional expansion and expects earnings to return to the growth path later this year as start-up-related costs ease and its newly launched in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) centres begin to contribute to profit.
After a strong finish in its financial year ended May 31, 2025 (FY2025), the company, which debuted on the ACE Market in March 2024, saw net profit for the first half of FY2026 fall 7.5% year on year to RM27.28 million, primarily due to higher pre-operating expenses tied to its expansion drive. Revenue, however, rose 15.3% to RM99.4 million, underscoring resilient demand, particularly from foreign patients.
Alpha IVF executive director and group managing director Datuk Dr Colin Lee Soon Soo (picture) believes the worst of the start-up drag is over.
“Pre-operating expenses such as renovations, talent acquisition, staff training and brand-building typically run for about a year before a centre becomes fully operational. With two new centres in Kota Kinabalu and Manila having commenced operations in December 2025, those costs are now largely behind us. Going forward, we expect these centres to contribute positively to both the top and bottom lines,” Lee tells The Edge in an interview.
The additions bring Alpha IVF’s total number of full-fledged IVF centres to six. As at end-2025, the group was operating four centres, one each in Petaling Jaya, Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Singapore, alongside two sales offices in Shanghai and Guangzhou and a satellite clinic in Jakarta.
That said, expansion-related costs will not disappear entirely. Three more centres, in Johor, Luzon and Bali, are currently under renovation or construction.
Setting up a full-fledged IVF centre costs between RM10 million and RM13 million, Lee says. Historically, most centres break even within the first month or quarter of operations, although overseas ventures may take longer as seen with Manila.
“Manila is our first overseas centre, so there are operational and regulatory nuances we’re still learning about, ” he adds.
Despite near-term cost pressures, Alpha IVF remains committed to expansion, both domestically and across Southeast Asia.
“We haven’t finished expanding. In fact, we probably never will. But as more centres become profitable, they will support new ones, reducing the margin impact from future openings,” Lee says. By end-November 2027, the group expects to operate eight centres.
In Indonesia, the group is developing a major centre in Bali’s Healthcare Special Economic Zone in Sanur, with operations targeted for mid-2027. Alpha IVF holds a 75% stake in the centre via its wholly-owned subsidiary Alpha IVF Systems Sdn Bhd, with the remaining 25% owned by local partner PT Delemont Global Venture.
In the Philippines, renovations are set to begin on a second facility in Tuguegarao, northern Luzon, serving a big market of more than 23 million people. The centre is expected to be operational by August 2026.
“Our ambition is to extend effective and efficient fertility services to as many people as possible, not just Malaysians, but also couples across the region. To do that, we need physical presence and strong branding,” Lee says.
Net profit in 1HFY2026 was also affected by Malaysia’s implementation of the 6% Sales and Service Tax (SST) on foreign patients from September 2025.
For Chinese patients, Alpha IVF chose to fully absorb the tax following agent requests for more time to adjust the pricing. As a result, earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margins and net profit were impacted in the September to November 2025 quarter, Lee says.
Indonesian patients, meanwhile, bore the full tax burden, compounded by a 14% depreciation of the rupiah against the ringgit over the past year. “That’s effectively a 20% increase in cost, which led some Indonesian patients to defer their visits,” he notes.
Still, Lee views the pullback as temporary. “Malaysia remains significantly more affordable than Singapore. Once patients adjust to the new pricing reality, we expect Indonesian patient volumes to return stronger than ever this year.”
Lee is cautiously optimistic that the second half of FY2026 will be strong enough to offset the decline in first-half earnings. He notes that the third quarter of its fiscal year is traditionally the weakest due to the Chinese New Year and Hari Raya Puasa festivals.
However, two factors could soften the seasonal slowdown this year. First, the two centres that commenced operations in December 2025 are now contributing to group results. Second, demand from Chinese patients hoping to conceive in the Year of the Horse is expected to support volumes.
The fourth quarter, typically the group’s strongest, is expected to see a rebound as start-up-related pressures on Ebitda and net profit margins ease further. “With many cost pressures reduced, I’m hopeful FY2026 will be a better year overall,” Lee says.
Bloomberg-compiled analyst estimates project net profit of RM59.2 million for FY2026, followed by an acceleration to RM82.2 million in FY2027 and RM98.3 million in FY2028. Alpha IVF posted a record net profit of RM57.5 million in FY2025, driven largely by its Malaysian operations, which accounted for nearly 89% of revenue.
Lee cites two structural tailwinds underpinning long-term demand. The first is demographic: couples are marrying later and delaying childbirth, a trend reinforced by rising urbanisation and socioeconomic advancement.
The second is Malaysia’s designation of 2026 as both Visit Malaysia Year 2026 and the Malaysia Year of Medical Tourism, with VMY2026 alone targeting 47 million international visitors — a potential boost for medical tourism demand, including IVF services.
While public discourse increasingly points to a growing number of people choosing not to have children, Lee believes this trend will not materially undermine Alpha IVF’s growth prospects, particularly in emerging markets.
“In countries like Indonesia and the Philippines, the population is young, and many are entering the reproductive age,” he says.
Industry benchmarks suggest demand for one IVF cycle per 800 people. Applied to Indonesia’s population of about 280 million, that implies potential demand of roughly 360,000 cycles annually versus just 13,000 currently performed. Malaysia, too, remains under-penetrated, performing only about 10,000 cycles annually against an estimated need for 40,000.
Lee says Alpha IVF selects markets based on demand, competitiveness, economics and geopolitical considerations.
“We not only look at local demand, but also at health tourism flow. That’s why we chose Kota Kinabalu. Beyond local demand, it has strong appeal to East Asian tourists and patients from surrounding regions, especially as flight connectivity improves.”
Competitive intensity is another key factor. In markets such as Thailand, IVF standards and success rates are already very high, making differentiation difficult.
“In Thailand, the specialists are very good. When we go there, we don’t necessarily stand out. But in markets where IVF outcomes are less consistent, our expertise is immediately recognised, making it easier to compete and sustain the business,” Lee notes.
Margins also play a decisive role. Alpha IVF has prioritised the Philippines and Indonesia over Vietnam, where lower procedure pricing compresses profitability. “In the Philippines and Indonesia, margins are more attractive. In Vietnam, IVF costs are low and margins are thin,” Lee says.
Indonesia offers an additional advantage: tax incentives. The government actively encourages foreign medical providers to establish operations in designated special economic zones, improving returns on investment.
Geopolitical risk also guides expansion. Alpha IVF had previously considered expansion into Cambodia and Laos, once popular IVF destinations for Chinese patients. However, tightening regulations and rising safety concerns following recent high-profile scams and crimes prompted the group to pivot instead to the Philippines, where partnerships and doctor recruitment were more straightforward, Lee says.
Alpha IVF remains self-funded, having maintained a net cash position since FY2022. As at end-November 2025, its cash balance stood at RM31.99 million and its short-term investments at RM105.68 million.
“So far, all the projects we’ve committed to can be funded without any external borrowing. We still have IPO (initial public offering) proceeds earmarked for expansion and beyond that, our internally generated cash flow remains healthy,” says Lee.
Alpha IVF raised RM116.64 million in its IPO in March 2024. At end-November 2025, RM62.96 million of it remained unutilised, a position Lee says reflects prudence rather than delayed execution.
While organic growth remains a priority, the group continues to evaluate merger and acquisition opportunities on a selective basis. “We’ve reviewed several opportunities in Malaysia and the region, but so far none has been suitable. There’s no mandate to acquire for the sake of it. If you force timing, you risk making the wrong decision,” he says.
On talent, Lee says Alpha IVF is well positioned to support growth, with no immediate bottlenecks in recruiting skilled medical specialists. “Across the group, we have 228 employees and 31 doctors and our doctors still have the capacity to take on more patients.”
Alpha IVF’s plan to migrate from the ACE Market to Bursa Malaysia’s Main Market has been delayed following changes to Securities Commission Malaysia’s guidelines, which now require companies to be listed for more than two years before applying.
“It’s a bit painful to think that we actually qualify in terms of dividends and fundamentals,” he says. Lee, 67, remains Alpha IVF’s largest shareholder, holding a 44.51% stake as at Jan 27, 2026.
The group maintains a dividend policy of at least 60% of net profit and has consistently exceeded this. It paid FY2024 dividends of 1.148 sen per share, FY2025 dividends of one sen per share and an interim 1HFY2026 dividend of 0.5 sen per share. Payout ratios were 100.6%, 84.6% and 89.1%, respectively.
Despite this, the stock closed at 27.5 sen last Friday — 14% below the IPO price of 32 sen — giving the group a market capitalisation of RM1.3 billion.
At its listing, Alpha IVF was valued at 21.2 times to 26 times forward earnings. Lee rejects suggestions that the IPO was overpriced. “Given our expansion trajectory, technological strength and the nature of the IVF sector, which has relatively high barriers to entry compared with general healthcare or hospital groups, the valuation was fair. If anything, we’re now cheaper and offer a better entry point,” he says.
The three analysts covering the stock rate it a “buy” with an average target price of 40 sen, implying 45% upside potential. AskEdge data shows peers trade at significantly higher multiples. The group trades at an average price-earnings ratio (PER) of 24.2 times, compared with Metro Healthcare Bhd’s (KL: METRO ) 71.1 times and TMC Life Sciences Bhd’s (KL: TMCLIFE ) 164.5 times. Larger hospital operators IHH Healthcare Bhd (KL: IHH ) and KPJ Healthcare Bhd (KL: KPJ ) trade at average PER of 34.6 times and 35 times respectively.
Lee believes the disconnect between fundamentals and valuation is temporary and that consistent earnings growth, capital discipline and an eventual migration to the Main Market will narrow the gap.

title: Nintendo’s profit disappoints even as memory prices climb
body:
(Feb 3): Nintendo Co’s profit rose a smaller-than-expected 23%, hurt by US tariffs on its flagship Switch 2 console and raising concerns about the impact of soaring memory chip prices on margins in 2026.
Switch 2 sales came to 7.01 million units in the December quarter, compared with the 6.5 million average analysts’ estimate. But operating income was ¥155.21 billion (US$998.5 million or RM3.92 billion), missing estimates for ¥180.7 billion. Sales leapt more than 80% to ¥806.32 billion, also below estimates.
After a record-setting summer debut for the Switch 2, the Kyoto-based company is grappling with global trade disruptions from US tariffs. Sales at home, where Nintendo priced its device intentionally low to hook consumers, took up a bigger proportion of business during the holiday quarter. Longer term, the Japanese company has to cope with surging memory prices that threaten the gadget’s already razor-thin margins. While most electronics makers, including Nintendo, have been protected by long-term supply contracts, that cushion is only temporary.
“Switch 2 sales figures can be seen as okay, but it would be hard to call them solid,” Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda said. Nintendo’s costs have risen in part because of stronger sales of the console in Japan and the impact of tariffs. “Looking ahead, concerns such as rising component prices remain, and how the company will once again control costs will be the key point to watch.”
Nintendo kept its full-year guidance for ¥2.25 trillion in revenue and ¥370 billion in operating profit, as well as Switch 2 unit sales of 19 million.
This year is pivotal for the new console’s long-term growth, as the size of its installed base will determine how much attention it attracts from third-party developers and gamers in the years that follow.
Chipmakers have been allocating more resources to far more lucrative advanced memory needed in AI data centres, raising the risk that Nintendo may struggle to even secure enough chips to manufacture the console, according to research firm TrendForce.
That’s resulting in rising memory prices that may also hurt software sales, Nintendo’s primary profit engine.
The Switch 2’s internal storage is limited to 256 gigabytes of memory, well below that of Sony Group Corp’s PlayStation 5 or Microsoft Corp’s Xbox. That’s as games increasingly require more firepower.
Big-budget titles such as Square Enix Holdings Co’s Final Fantasy VII Remake can consume more than 90 gigabytes, forcing users to purchase MicroSD Express cards to expand storage. Prices for those cards are also climbing, partly due to AI-driven demand for solid-state drives, which could further discourage game purchases.
Nintendo may seek ways to improve hardware profitability while sustaining consumer interest through measures such as releasing Switch 2 models in different colours. Still, component price rises are expected to persist through at least 2026 and may test the company’s ability to absorb them.
That said, it would be a mistake to dismiss the enduring appeal of the intellectual property of Mario creator, according to Bernstein analyst Robin Zhu.
“The ecosystem is doing okay,” he said. “The majority of the miss came in operating expenses. Not to say that’s good, but it’s less bad of a problem than if demand had gone very wrong, which has been the narrative for a while while the stock sold off.”

title: Cover Story 2: National Gas Roadmap to overhaul gas policy amid tightening supply, coal phase-out by 2044
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on February 2, 2026 - February 8, 2026
MALAYSIA’s National Gas Roadmap (NGR), slated for release by the third quarter this year, is shaping up to be the most consequential reset of the country’s natural gas ecosystem since liberalisation began almost a decade ago. It is expected to redefine how natural gas is priced, supplied and regulated nationwide, as well as align federal and state policies across Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak.
At the centre of the road map is a longstanding structural issue: Malaysia’s gas reserves and infrastructure are unevenly distributed, and state rights — particularly in Sabah and Sarawak — are not peripheral factors but core determinants of policy direction.
Newly minted Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir says the NGR will formalise Malaysia’s shift towards natural gas as both a transition fuel and a strategic resource.
While the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR) projects coal to be “close to fully phased out” by 2050, the minister has committed to a faster timeline.
“We are targeting to reduce half of the [coal] capacity by 2035 and there will be no more coal generation by 2044,” Akmal tells The Edge in an interview. “So far, that would be the timeline we are looking at … that’s the commitment.”
The road map will determine whether Malaysia can balance that coal exit against shrinking gas reserves, rising demand and the need to diversify supply — including preparing Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah for higher liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports — while preserving competitiveness and managing the realities of state-federal energy governance.
Malaysia’s gas reserves are declining at a rate that raises long-term security concerns, with sharper depletion in Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah, where annual output has contracted by an estimated 7% and 4%, respectively, according to reports. In comparison, Sarawak — which accounts for about 59% of Malaysia’s total gas reserves — has a high and stable supply.
At the same time, the NETR projects natural gas to account for 56% of Malaysia’s total primary energy supply by 2050, up from 43% in 2020. The combination of rising dependence and tightening domestic supply points to a structural conclusion: The country will need to increase LNG imports, particularly for Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah.
Akmal does not explicitly say Malaysia — now the world’s fifth-largest LNG exporter after Russia, Qatar, Australia and the US — will become a net LNG importer, but his remarks indicate that the NGR is being designed with that trajectory in mind.
“When we talk about the security of the [gas] supply, we definitely need to look into the mechanism for third-party importers. And in order for it to happen, we definitely need to invest in our infrastructure. We need to upgrade the pipeline [network] and also the regasification terminals,” he says.
The NGR is also expected to address a long-standing barrier to investment: domestic gas price controls. These controls were designed to preserve affordability but have had the unintended effect of dampening upstream and midstream investment. They have also discouraged new importers from supplying LNG to the domestic market.
“The known issue for our gas market is that the price control for the domestic [market] has not been viable or has not attracted investments,” Akmal says.
Pressed whether this points towards the liberalisation of the domestic market, he says the matter “will be addressed in the NGR. What I can say is that we are looking into price controls and the need to upgrade the facilities”.
He stops short of confirming full liberalisation but signals that structural reform is unavoidable.
Malaysia began opening its gas market in 2017 through third-party access (TPA), which allows licensed importers and shippers to use the country’s gas facilities. Uptake, however, has been modest. Several LNG import and shipping licences have been issued since 2019, yet none of the licensees imported cargo until 2024, when E&H Energy secured a 20-year supply agreement with Mexico’s Amigo LNG, a subsidiary of Singapore-based LNG Alliance.
The government has also ended regulated prices for the non-power sector, with the Malaysia Reference Price now serving as the market benchmark. While prices for the power sector remain regulated until at least end-2027, they are increasingly influenced by global price trends.
Existing long-term contracts between Petroliam Nasional Bhd and major power-sector buyers such as Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL: TENAGA ) and the independent power producers continue to limit incentives for these players to turn to alternative suppliers. This dampens competition even though the legal framework for TPA is already in place.
Sabah and Sarawak control most of Malaysia’s remaining gas reserves and have expanded their authority over infrastructure and downstream development in recent years, making any national planning exercise impossible without their buy-in.
Akmal stresses that the road map was developed with both states involved through the National Energy Council and direct stakeholder consultations led by the ministry of economy.
Two long-running issues — Sabah’s claims over revenue and Sarawak’s control over gas distribution — continue to sit at the centre of state-federal negotiations. These matters, he says, are being addressed through the MA63 Implementation Action Council.
“The NGR is a comprehensive national road map that harmonises policies between the federal and state governments to ensure coordinated and effective implementation nationwide,” he says. “Therefore, the implementation of NGR is expected to be meaningfully executed.”
Investment needs add another layer of complexity. The NETR estimates RM1.2 trillion to RM1.3 trillion will be required for the overall energy transition by 2050, with RM630 billion earmarked for renewables alone, according to Akmal.
“We are on track with the targets we set, but the landscape is dynamic. The further we advance the energy transition, the more investments are being drawn to Malaysia.”
The NGR will sit within that wider investment push and is expected to outline capital requirements for upstream competitiveness, expansion of regasification and pipeline capacity, and a more flexible, market-based downstream system.

title: Martin Schulz succeeds Amanda Zhang as CEO of Mercedes-Benz Cars Malaysia
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Feb 3): Amid a leadership transition in its Southeast Asia operations, Mercedes-Benz Cars Malaysia on Tuesday announced the appointment of Martin Schulz as its new CEO and president, effective Feb 1.
According to the press statement issued by Mercedes-Benz Malaysia Sdn Bhd — a wholly-owned subsidiary of Mercedes-Benz AG — on Tuesday, Schulz has also been appointed head of a newly integrated Southeast Asian region, encompassing four key markets, namely Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
He succeeds Amanda Zhang, who will remain on the board of directors and serve as a senior adviser to the automotive firm.
Over her two-decade career with Mercedes-Benz, Zhang has held senior leadership roles across Europe and Southeast Asia, guiding organisations through major transformation.
In Malaysia, she spearheaded Southeast Asia’s first Retail of the Future agency model and launched the flagship luxury retail format Stars @ Mercedes-Benz Bangsar.
Her tenure also saw the expansion of the electric vehicle (EV) charging ecosystem, profitable growth in Singapore and a strengthened regional go-to-market strategy.
These initiatives positioned the business for sustained growth, accelerated electrification and long-term customer value creation, Mercedes-Benz Malaysia said.
In her advisory role, Zhang will support strategic continuity and ensure a seamless transition.
“It has been a privilege to lead Mercedes-Benz Malaysia and Singapore, and I am immensely proud of what our team has achieved across the region. I warmly welcome Martin Schulz into this pivotal role and have full confidence in his leadership as he drives the next phase of growth in Southeast Asia,” Zhang said in a press release.
Schulz, who joined Mercedes-Benz in 1999, brings extensive international experience. He previously served as CEO in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Romania, and has held senior management roles of more than 10 years in Vietnam, Thailand and Korea.
Most recently, he was based at Mercedes-Benz headquarters in Stuttgart, in charge of various sales and marketing functions.
“I am thrilled to return to Asia and lead our teams in Malaysia and across Southeast Asia. This is a period of immense opportunity, and I look forward to working closely with colleagues and retail partners to deliver exceptional customer experiences and reinforce our leadership in luxury mobility,” said Schulz.

title: China silver fund revaluation sparks 31% drop, investor pushback
body:
(Feb 3): UBS SDIC Fund Management Co changed the valuation model for a US$2.2 billion (RM8.72 billion) silver fund to more closely track global futures prices, triggering a record drop in its net asset value and outcry among investors already bruised by a precious metals slump.
The UBS SDIC Silver Futures Fund LOF will be valued based on prices in silver futures on major global markets instead of those listed at the Shanghai Futures Exchange, according to statements from UBS SDIC. The change, which came into effect on Monday (Feb 2), led to a record 31.5% drop in the product’s net asset value.
UBS SDIC, a joint venture between the Swiss bank and a unit of State Development and Investment Group Co, said in a statement that it strives “to timely and fairly reflect the true value in assets”.
Last month’s rally in precious metals came to a halt on Friday when spot silver prices plunged more than 25%. Investors had been piling into commodities amid renewed concerns about geopolitical upheaval and threats to the US Federal Reserve’s independence.
The LOF fund mainly invests in silver futures listed on the Shanghai bourse, which are bound by a 17% daily limit, while global futures markets have no price caps.
The drop marks one of the sharpest single-day declines for Chinese mutual funds.
The adjustment came as silver futures on the Comex tumbled 32.7% in the prior two sessions as a frenzied rally, partly fuelled by Chinese speculators, ground to a halt. It has also sparked an outcry on social media. Any investor who tried to redeem the funds late Monday would incur an extra loss with the revaluation.
UBS SDIC said the recent market upheaval, with global futures price declines far exceeding the 17% limit, meant the fund’s net asset value can’t fully and timely reflect the fair value in its underlying assets under the previous model, according to a statement on its public WeChat account. It will resume referencing the silver settlement prices in Shanghai for valuation once the underlying futures contracts “reflect the characteristics of active trading markets”.
Unadjusted valuation would allow investors that redeem at an earlier time to exit at an inflated net asset value and expose remaining investors to the risk of asset prices returning to their true value, which the firm said is “obviously against the principle of fairness”.
After precious metals from gold to silver unravelled last week, the Shanghai Futures Exchange on Monday urged member institutions to beef up risk management and to remind investors to participate rationally.

title: Builder-turned-blogger Koon Yew Yin passes away
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Feb 3): Koon Yew Yin, who co-founded Malaysia’s largest construction firms including Gamuda Bhd (KL: GAMUDA ), passed away on Monday at the age of 93.
Born in 1933, Koon is one of the 12 children of a coffin shop owner. He studied at St John’s Institution in Kuala Lumpur and graduated with a diploma in civil engineering from the Technical College that is now known as Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.
He started his career as an engineer with the Public Works Department in the newly independent Malaya. In 1967, he established Mudajaya Construction Sdn Bhd and Gamuda Sdn Bhd together with three partners.
IGB Construction Sdn Bhd, Jurutama Construction Sdn Bhd and Mudajaya Construction Sdn Bhd merged in 1983 to become IJM Corporation Bhd (KL: IJM ), which was listed five years later with a market capitalisation of RM66 million. Today, IJM is worth nearly RM10 billion.
Gamuda, meanwhile, is Malaysia’s biggest construction firm by revenue with a market value of some RM25 billion.
Koon retired from corporate life in 1983 after suffering serious heart angina and turned his attention to investing.
He often recalled the 1983-84 Hong Kong stock market crash, triggered by fears of China reclaiming the territory. While many investors fled, Koon embraced contrarian investing — buying when others were fearful and selling when others rushed in.
Starting with RM200,000 in cash, he bought undervalued stocks such as Hong Kong Realty and Trust Ltd, which rebounded dramatically. He indicated making more than 200% profit on his initial shares before reinvesting the proceeds into higher-value counters like HSBC.
His capital eventually grew large enough to acquire a 46% stake in Kaiser Stock and Shares Ltd, a Hong Kong stockbroking company.
Koon has also written regularly about stock investments, market trends, and corporate governance on his personal website as well as on investment portal i3 .
Known by his initials “KYY” among fans and detractors, Koon became a prolific blogger on i3 investment portal, posting views on stock investments, market trends, and corporate governance. His candid insights made him a familiar and sometimes controversial voice in Malaysia’s investment community.
He began blogging as early as February 2016, with posts ranging from personal reflections such as What makes me happy to detailed investment commentaries. His entries continued through late 2025 and early 2026.
He has admitted to losing considerable sums after using margin finance to buy shares in KSL Holdings Bhd (KL: KSL ), a property developer he considered undervalued, and how he was forced to sell his shares in JAKS Resources Bhd (KL: JAKS ) to meet margin calls.
Koon’s career was not without controversy.
He was one of the founders of Beh Minerals Sdn Bhd, which held a 35% stake in Asian Rare Earth Sdn Bhd, a joint venture with a Japanese company to extract rare earth yttrium in Bukit Merah, Perak.
However, the factory generated serious radioactive health damage and environmental pollution, sparking massive public protests that prompted the government to step in and halt its operations. There were seven deaths as a result of the pollution as well as birth defects and leukaemia cases reported within five years in a community of 11,000 people.
After a protracted legal battle, the Japanese partner agreed to settle for RM10 million on the condition that the compensation was only to be used for charity, resulting in the creation of Yayasan Teratai in Ipoh, Perak.
Koon has also established scholarships and contributed generously to universities, including RM1 million annual student grant to Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman, driven by his belief that education was the key to uplifting society.
His philanthropy extended beyond financial support. Koon often spoke about the transformative power of education, urging young Malaysians to pursue knowledge as a means of empowerment. His commitment to education reflected his broader philosophy of social responsibility and fairness.

title: Manage currency risks through appropriate hedging, business strategies, Miti minister tells companies
body:
KUALA LUMPUR (Feb 3): Companies must actively manage currency risks through appropriate hedging and business strategies, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.
He said fluctuations in the ringgit are a normal market occurrence and part of the broader economic cycle, with their impact differing across sectors depending on business models and market exposure.
“While currency movements may create challenges for some, they also present opportunities for others. What is important is for businesses to manage currency risks effectively by adopting appropriate strategies such as hedging, supply chain protection and customer management,” he said.
He said this when asked by reporters about the strengthening of the ringgit last week, which, for the first time in seven years, reached the 3.9 level against the US dollar, at the official launch of the GD XCHANGE Experience Centre here on Tuesday.
Johari said the impact of currency movements depends on the type of business, noting that, for example, commodities and consumer-related businesses require different approaches to managing currency risks.
On Malaysia’s decision to sign the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the US, he said the move was a pragmatic step aimed at avoiding higher tariffs and safeguarding the country’s economic interests.
“Signing the agreement provides Malaysia with space and time to negotiate the terms, while failure to do so could have resulted in immediate tariff hikes that would affect exports and the broader economy.
“The government had carefully weighed the costs and benefits before signing, and it should be noted that the agreement includes an exit clause should it no longer serve Malaysia’s interests,” he said.
The priority, he added, is to ensure that businesses operating in Malaysia are protected and that the economy remains resilient.
Meanwhile, GDEX Bhd (KL: GDEX ) managing director and group chief executive officer Teong Teck Lean said the stronger ringgit is generally positive for the group.
“A stronger ringgit helps reduce costs for services priced in the US dollar, such as software licences and technology subscriptions, making them more affordable compared with periods when the ringgit was weaker.
“From a talent perspective, a firmer ringgit could also help with retention, as the wage gap between Malaysia and neighbouring markets narrows slightly, reducing the incentive for talent to move abroad,” he said at a press conference after the launch.
He added that a stronger ringgit is welcome, as it supports cost efficiency, particularly on the technology side, with no major downside to the group’s core operations.
Also present at the launch was GDEX chairman Tan Sri Muhammad Ibrahim.
GD XCHANGE is the technology arm of GDEX, representing the group’s transformation from a conventional courier and logistics provider into a fully integrated, technology-driven logistics and distribution ecosystem.
GD XCHANGE brings together global technology principals, channel partners, and resellers across key areas, including supply chain and commerce, cybersecurity, cloud subscriptions, workspace solutions, smart devices and connectivity, and the electric vehicle ecosystem.

title: Cover Story 2: Making haste in engineering Malaysia’s growth path
body:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on February 2, 2026 - February 8, 2026
NOT many people would have envied Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir’s appointment as minister of economy in Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim’s third cabinet line-up in December 2025. After all, he would have a two-year window, at most, to execute the reform agenda as the 16th general election (GE16) needs to be held by February 2028 — that is, if the PM does not call for a snap election.
Therefore, the two-term member of parliament for Johor Bahru, who is with the Anwar-led Parti Keadilan Rakyat, had to hit the ground running.
First up are two economic outlines: the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) Blueprint and Masterplan, which is expected to be unveiled by end-March to guide development; and the Natural Gas Roadmap (NGR) in the second or third quarter of this year to prepare for longer-term industry realities.
Existing master plans, road maps and policies, such as the National Energy Transition Roadmap (NETR), New Industrial Master Plan 2030 (NIMP 2030), Bumiputera Economic Transformation Plan 2035 and the progressive wage policy, will also have to be carried out.
In addition, the five-year period of the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP) started on Jan 1, 2026, and Akmal will be the first minister of economy to oversee its implementation. All these plans are pillars in Anwar’s Madani Economic Framework.
While these master plans, road maps and policies have long-term trajectories — for example, the NETR is aimed at achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 — the failure of any of these programmes could be attributed to Akmal and be politically damaging to him. What can he realistically achieve in two years?
“Well, if you frame it from that perspective, even with the time constraint, I think it makes things easier because I know [there need to be priorities],” Akmal tells The Edge in his office at Menara Prisma in Putrajaya.
Assuming the office vacated by maverick politician Datuk Seri Rafizi Ramli is no small feat. After all, during his 2½ years in office, Rafizi introduced many of those policies, some of which were identified as his projects.
Akmal, who is eight years younger than Rafizi (incidentally, their birthdays are just two days apart), says he will focus on executing the policies and tasks that need to be carried out for the sake of the economy and the people, rather than attempting to make a mark for himself.
“For me, it is not about building my legacy. It is about delivering what is right for the country,” says Akmal, who turns 40 on Malaysia Day this year.
“And for me, even though I’m young, I need to show maturity. It’s okay to continue the good programmes. And when we say it’s okay to continue, we will definitely need to ensure the effectiveness of those plans in 2026.”
He sees his predecessor as the architect and himself as the engineer who will see to the implementation of 13MP, as well as the various economic road maps and blueprints. This is going to be the year of executing those plans, he declares.
“It is unique to look from the [perspective of the] whole ecosystem, whereby now the building blocks and architecture are already there. Now it is time for us to come up with [the execution plan],” says Akmal.
“I consider myself the engineer, [looking at] how to put all the blocks, all the pieces together so we can make the breakthrough where finally Malaysia can move up in this high-end, high-value industry.”
Besides finalising the JS-SEZ Blueprint and Masterplan, the Ministry of Economy will also develop a social economy policy and regulatory framework to bring the third sector (social enterprises, non-profit organisations and cooperatives) into the mainstream, as well as complete the NETR Impact Study and the development of the Integrated Circuit Design Parks.
The country will also host the KL20 Summit to strengthen Malaysia’s position as a vibrant destination for start-ups and venture capital, implement the Malaysia Blue Economy Blueprint and conduct several studies to strengthen national food production hubs and supply chains along the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak.
The ministry will also come up with the National Ageing Blueprint this year.
The need to get the narrative right on the economy and to get all stakeholders on the same page in terms of policies and initiatives are high on Akmal’s priority list with investors looking closely at how Malaysia executes the 13MP and JS-SEZ.
He will deliver the opening remarks at the Forum Ekonomi Malaysia (FEM) in Kuala Lumpur on Feb 5. In its second year, the forum brings together leaders and experts to discuss the pressing issues and outlook that will shape the country’s economic landscape.
“We know, for example, there are few policies and initiatives that have been announced, for example, JS-SEZ. The framework is there, but for this year, everyone expects the blueprint. It is going to be about the operational period,” says Akmal.
While the success of the JS-SEZ will depend on the good bilateral relationship between Malaysia and Singapore, there is still need for clarity in terms of how Malaysia can really lock in the investments from interested parties coming to gauge prospects, he adds.
The JS-SEZ Blueprint and Masterplan are expected to be unveiled by the end of March. The documents will include a practical and actionable road map to operationalise the JS-SEZ.
The documents will serve as a guide for the government and stakeholders in translating their ambitions into execution, while providing clarity and confidence to investors, the Ministry of Economy tells The Edge. “Importantly, they will articulate a clear value proposition — outlining opportunities, incentives and the operational framework of the JS-SEZ over the next 10 to 20 years,” it adds.
On the reason for the delay of the blueprint, Akmal would only say that Rafizi had pushed for the blueprint to be unveiled by the fourth quarter of 2025, but the Ministry of Economy needed “to get a clear decision on it”. “[It was already December] by the time we had the cabinet reshuffle [but] things are clearer in terms of how we are going to bring the matter forward,” he adds.
Akmal says the additional time to roll out the blueprint gives him the chance to level up with his Singapore counterpart and iron out remaining gaps. “I think in terms of issues or challenges that we need to address, we need to really strengthen and allow for stronger coordination — especially if it involves many agencies on our side as well as on the other side.”
Being the MP for Johor Bahru allows him to offer some views and insights on the city to be included in the JS-SEZ Blueprint, to ensure that the programmes and initiatives will also be felt by the locals, he says. “In that sense [the delay of the blueprint] was fortunate … because before it is revealed, being the minister, I have a say in it,” he adds.
According to Akmal, there is a need for clarity on several ongoing initiatives such as the strategic partnership with ARM Holdings, a UK-based chip architecture company, in the licensing of the company’s advanced semiconductor design blueprints.
The agreement, which is spread over 10 years and includes training for 10,000 local engineers, is aimed at fostering local chip firms and bolstering exports of more than RM1.2 trillion by 2030 by transitioning Malaysia from back-end chip assembly and testing to higher-value chip design. However, there are concerns that the deal risks being underutilised as there are too few companies in Malaysia able to design advanced chips.
However, Akmal says the deal has attracted interest from local players as well as foreign companies looking to set up operations here. He says the deal is a new opportunity for the industry as it cannot develop without access to the intellectual property for chip architecture.
“That is why the fact that we managed to sign a deal between the government and the company opens doors for our players to gain access,” says Akmal, letting on that he intends to announce some progress on the ARM partnership during FEM. He adds that the technology provided by ARM is dynamic in the sense that it is not going to be stuck at the level of chips in 2026.
The ministry is currently going through the requirements, looking at the capabilities of the applicants to not only deliver the product, but also make sure the chips can actually be used by their clients, says Akmal.
While the aim of the partnership with ARM is for Malaysia’s chip design companies to eventually come up with their own advanced designs and push the country’s semiconductor industry up the value chain, it is also about retaining talents in the country.
“For foreign entities to set up here in Malaysia, for them to have the assets, we also put in the requirement to ensure local talents will be used [and involve local players] throughout the value chain. So, in that sense, I think progress has been made. We are in the midst of deciding who is going to be among the first few recipients so that this can start moving,” says Akmal.
More than 10 applications have been received for access to the ARM chip infrastructure, he says. “But definitely, we have to scrutinise [the applicants] in terms of their capability, to ensure it’s not just about accessing the technology, but the commitment to actually producing our own design — made by Malaysia,” he says.
Malaysia’s investment aspirations in the semiconductor industry are outlined in the National Semiconductor Strategy (NSS) launched in May 2024 by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti).
While it is not directly under the purview of the Ministry of Economy, the semiconductor industry, being the backbone of Malaysia’s manufacturing sector, is of particular importance to the government as a whole.
The NSS outlines a RM500 billion investment plan designed to elevate the semiconductor industry’s capabilities from a back-end assembly hub to a global powerhouse in integrated circuit design, advanced packaging and front-end fabrication. The government has committed RM25 billion in fiscal support to foster local champions, including direct spending of RM10 billion in capital grants and RM3.25 billion in training and research and development (R&D).
The Ministry of Economy is one of the implementing ministries and agencies of the NSS, especially in terms of the RM10 billion in capital grants that the government will provide over 10 to 16 years. However, there are grouses that the R&D spending is not enough to achieve the targets outlined under the NSS, which includes establishing at least 10 Malaysian companies specialising in design and advanced packaging, with each generating revenue of between RM1 billion and RM4.7 billion.
On this, Akmal says he is going to assess those claims to see if there is a need to streamline public investments in R&D to ensure its effectiveness. “We will definitely spend on R&D, but the question is: Is it enough? Is it at the right focus? Is it in the right industry? This is where I think at least, we can start zooming in to be more hands-on.”
Malaysia has been a bright spot for data centre investments in recent years, owing to the availability of land, competitive electricity and water rates for industrial users as well as Singapore’s initial ban on such investments. The country became more selective on data centre investments after concerns about pressure on water-related infrastructure, especially in Johor. Miti has come up with updated regulations on the sustainability of data centre investments.
On its role in charting the course of economic development, the Ministry of Economy is looking at how the country can move into higher-value products and services in artificial intelligence (AI), leveraging the data centre investments that the country has been receiving.
As data centres require a lot of advanced processing units and servers, Malaysia is looking to benefit from those requirements by focusing on upgrading its semiconductor technology and industry through the NSS, especially its partnership with ARM.
“That’s why I think everything will fall into place. For example, one of the components will be chips for the server or CPU unit … all these data centres, when they need to upgrade their servers, we cannot be relying on just imports. From the economy ministry’s perspective, this is where we can start inserting our high-value products,” says Akmal.
The ministry will also provide more clarity on how exactly the government is addressing the issue of brain drain, as well as employment opportunities and wages for young people, especially as the country’s population ages. Malaysia is already an ageing nation, with 7.7% of the population aged 65 years and over in 2024 — above the 7% threshold to be considered an ageing nation.
Akmal says the ministry is rolling out a blueprint that will focus on how technology such as AI can be deployed to address the issues relating to an ageing nation.
“The burden will be on the young as it forces dependence on our youth to support economic growth. So, I think it is not just about the needs to address the ageing population, but also how ready we are in terms of our young talents,” he adds.
“We have been talking about technology, we have been talking about AI, we talk a lot in terms of talents, so hopefully through all these initiatives and the efforts that are being continued, these will allow the perspective of the youth [to be included in the blueprint].”
One of the efforts to reform the labour market and increase workers’ income in line with productivity growth is through the progressive wage policy (PWP), which was piloted between June and August 2024. Under the PWP, the government will provide a monthly allowance of RM200 to RM300 per worker to participating employers to help offset the cost of salary increases.
According to the ministry, a total of 756 employers participated in the pilot programme. Of that number, 359 or 47% of employers had increased the wages of 3,710 workers in accordance with the guideline.
The total government expenditure for incentive payments under the PWP pilot programme was RM2.23 million. Under Budget 2025, the government allocated RM200 million to support the full implementation of the PWP in 2025, which would benefit 50,000 employees.
“Incentive payments will be disbursed to employers that have increased their employees’ wages until December 2027. As at Dec 31, 2025, 4,025 employers had participated in the PWP and increased the wages of 51,363 employees, exceeding the set target,” says the ministry.
One of the most visible programmes introduced by Akmal’s predecessor, Rafizi, is the central database hub or PADU, a platform that collates and integrates data on Malaysian households to help the government make better decisions when it comes to socioeconomic development and aid.
It was conceptualised by Rafizi so that the government would have a better overview of which segments of society that really need subsidies and other assistance, so that government spending on social programmes would be more targeted.
While the system received cabinet approval, it was later mired in concerns about data security as well as the political implications of having such streamlined data, plus fear of a potential backlash on targeted subsidies.
As a result, the data collated by PADU was not used to determine the eligibility for the purchase of RON95 petrol at the subsidised price of RM1.99 per litre under the BUDI95 programme. Instead, the government chose to give a generous quota of the fuel to all Malaysians, only removing subsidies for foreigners and businesses not entitled to preferential rates.
For now, other social assistance programmes such as the Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah for basic goods continue to be based on earnings level without taking into account other factors such as household size and spending needs. This repudiation of PADU has led to its relevance being questioned.
However, Akmal says the government will continue to use PADU, but it needs to explore how to capitalise on and leverage the data collated and refined by the system.
“Having all this data also opens up the opportunity for us to strengthen analytics for the government. So, it can be one of the references for the government to decide on certain policies. Hopefully by this quarter, we can announce the direction for PADU because that analytical tools may assist the government in making certain decisions on socioeconomic policies,” he adds.
While PADU seems to be relegated, the ministry claims that the inclusiveness and availability of the data enables it to offer data-as-a-service to government agencies, supporting them in formulating policies and evaluating the effectiveness of socioeconomic intervention programmes. PADU currently holds 30.7 million profiles of individuals and permanent residents in Malaysia.
“In the first quarter of 2025, the ministry moved forward with data sharing by offering data-as-a-service to government agencies. As a result, by December 2025, a total of 12 agencies had been approved to access the data in PADU,” says the ministry.
“These include, among others, the Ministry of Finance, the National Digital Department and the Institute for Youth Research Malaysia. The data has been utilised for purposes such as subsidy targeting, the validation and verification of social assistance programmes, and the digitalisation of government services.”
The ministry is gearing up to expand its PADU services to support the implementation of the 13MP. Further details on its direction and upcoming initiatives will be announced this month, it says.
The next two years will be critical not just for Akmal, but also the Anwar-led Madani government to show the people that they have what it takes to bring the nation forward. For his part, Akmal hopes to play the role of engineer well to ensure the various blueprints live up to promises made to the people and the country.

title: Samsung’s best day since 2008 powers South Korean stock rally
body:
(Feb 3): A global rush to secure memory chips for artificial intelligence (AI) is powering a renewed surge in South Korean equities, with chipmakers leading a rebound that pushed the Kospi to a fresh record on Tuesday.
Samsung Electronics Co shares jumped 11% on Korea Exchange, the most since 2008, while SK Hynix Inc added more than 9%. Both stocks recouped losses from the previous session. The benchmark Kospi climbed nearly 7%, extending its gain for the year to 25% and solidifying its status as the world’s best-performing equity index.
Up more than 39% each this year, the chip duo have continued to set new records as investors embrace AI’s voracious demand for memory chips. Despite the torrid gains, few analysts see them as expensive thanks to strong earnings momentum and still-reasonable valuations.
“The structural shortage in memory chips makes the continued growth of Samsung and SK Hynix inevitable,” said Kim Namho, a fund manager at Timefolio Investment Management in Seoul.
Trading is becoming more erratic as the chipmakers extend last year’s huge rallies, however, with the daily news flow spurring investors to sell one day and buy the next.
Risk appetite rebounded in Asia as markets got positive tailwinds from solid US factory data and a calming of the sell-off in precious metals. Sentiment had been hit in previous sessions as traders mulled the pick for the Federal Reserve chair along with ongoing worries on geopolitical tensions and the sustainability of the AI boom. South Korean stock volatility spiked to the highest since 2020 on Monday.
“We view yesterday’s volatility in the South Korean equity market as a healthy digestion of gains,” said Sojung Park, a portfolio manager at Matthews International Capital Management. “From an earnings growth and valuation perspective, we remain positive on South Korea.”
Local institutions were the main drivers of Tuesday’s bounce in Seoul, and foreign funds also bought stocks on a net basis, while retail investors sold. Buy orders for programme trading were briefly halted after Kospi 200 futures jumped more than 5%.
The rebound puts the Kospi back above the 5,000 target set last year by President Lee Jae Myung as part of a campaign to raise market valuations. The administration and regulators have pushed for improved corporate governance in an effort to win back global investors.
“Global attention on South Korea’s value‑up story isn’t fading anytime soon,” said James Lee, the head of global business at Must Asset Management in Seoul. “For the market to truly level up, though, this concentration in Samsung and SK Hynix needs to spill over into the broader market and lift the rest of the sectors as well.”
The South Korean market climbed to a valuation of over US$3.3 trillion (RM13.0 trillion) last week, overtaking Germany as the world’s 10th largest. The combined market capitalisation of Samsung and SK Hynix has reached more than US$1.1 trillion, surpassing the total value of Chinese tech giants Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Tencent Holdings Ltd.
JPMorgan Chase & Co strategists including Mixo Das raised their “bull case” Kospi target to 7,500 in a note on Monday. They see drivers beyond chips including defence and shipbuilding, with room for further company reforms and greater participation among investors at home and abroad.

title: GDEX says RM5 courier floor price largely ignored pending gazettement
body:
PETALING JAYA (Feb 3): Malaysian courier operators have largely ignored a RM5 floor price for parcel deliveries because it is not legally binding, GDEX Bhd (KL: GDEX ) managing director and group chief executive officer Teong Teck Lean said on Tuesday.
The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) introduced reference price guidelines for courier services in December 2024, but the proposal, including a RM5 minimum price for parcels weighing 2kg and below, has yet to be gazetted, leaving compliance voluntary.
“The RM5 reference price was announced, but it has not been gazetted,” Teong told reporters after the opening of GDEX’s GD XCHANGE Experience Centre by Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani here on Tuesday.
“I believe not many companies are actually following it.”
Teong said the lack of enforcement has resulted in uneven compliance across the industry, which has become increasingly competitive following the entry of large foreign-backed platforms over the past six to seven years.
“These players have taken the lion’s share of the market through aggressive pricing,” he said, adding that GDEX is shifting its focus towards the business-to-business segment, where service quality plays a bigger role than price alone.
The reference price guidelines were intended to promote sustainable pricing and fair competition in the courier sector. However, they will only become mandatory once formally gazetted.
Last November, Communications Minister Datuk Fahmi Fadzil said the government was studying a proposal to introduce a mandatory floor price for courier services, backed by cost audits and industry-wide feasibility studies, to ensure operator sustainability while balancing consumer costs.
As at Oct 15, MCMC had licensed 102 courier companies under the Postal Services Act 2012, comprising 21 foreign-owned and 81 locally owned operators. Industry data shows that 15 major licensees handle about 98% of total parcel volume, with Indonesia’s J&T Express and SPX Xpress (Shopee Express) together controlling 73.5% of the market.
Teong said the intense price competition had reinforced GDEX’s strategy to diversify into technology services, which now account for nearly 20% of group revenue.
“This is to hedge against over-dependence on a single segment,” he said, describing the move as a long-term strategy rather than a short-term shift.
Commenting on Japan’s Yamato Holdings Co Ltd, which in October 2025 trimmed its stake in GDEX to 19.637% from 23.242% after selling 200 million shares in a direct business transaction, Teong said the group’s operational relationship with Yamato remains intact.
“They are still a very good partner, and our collaboration continues,” he said.
GDEX shares rose half a sen, or 3.7%, to 14 sen by midday on Tuesday, valuing the company at about RM789.8 million. The stock is up 7.7% so far this year.
